skills.name: Parts of speech and a tense overview

note.text: A word’s class depends on its use: book is a noun in the book and a verb in book a room. Nouns name, verbs form the clause’s action or state, adjectives describe nouns and adverbs can modify actions or other expressions. Time and grammatical tense are related but not identical. Simple present often expresses habits; simple past presents completed past events. Progressive forms use be + -ing; perfect forms use have + past participle. This is an overview, not a claim that every form has only one meaning.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to identify word functions in context and distinguish common tense/aspect patterns. Builds on: Form Three’s sentence patterns and verb forms. Leads to: choosing accurate simple forms, clause patterns and narrative tenses.

sections.heading: Understand the pattern
sections.text: A word’s class depends on its use: book is a noun in the book and a verb in book a room. Simple present often expresses habits; simple past presents completed past events. Progressive forms use be + -ing; perfect forms use have + past participle. sections.heading: Read the original model
sections.text: Original capsule: Bih reads after chores: present habit. Yesterday she {past('write')} a note: simple past. She is {ing('read')} now: present progressive. She has {participle('write')} the note: present perfect. By the later meeting she had {participle('write')} it: past perfect. She will read tomorrow: future reference. Read the whole time context before choosing a form.

sections.heading: Apply and check
sections.text: Ask what the word does in this sentence, then identify the finite verb and any auxiliary. Do not label every -ly word an adverb without checking its function. A past participle is not automatically the same as the simple past. Later lessons practise particular contrasts in more depth.

cards.idea: Distinguish the ideas used in this lesson.
example: noun: a word naming an entity or idea in the stated use.
verb: a word functioning in the clause’s action or state pattern.
adjective: a word describing a noun in the stated pattern.
adverb: a word modifying how or when an action occurs in the stated pattern.

cards.idea: Read the whole example before identifying its function.
example: In the book is here, book names an object.
In book a room, book expresses the action.
In a quiet room, quiet describes room.
In Bih reads quietly, quietly modifies reads.

cards.idea: A correction must preserve the intended meaning and form.
example: Book must be a verb in every sentence. Correction: Word class depends on use; the book uses book as a noun.
A word’s spelling fixes one class in every use. Correction: The same spelling can have a different grammatical function.
Quiet in a quiet room modifies only a verb. Correction: It describes the noun room, so it is adjectival here.
Every adjective and adverb can be exchanged without changing the construction. Correction: Choose the form that fits what it modifies.

pick.q: Choose the action in progress now.
e: A finite auxiliary is missing.
The progressive needs -ing after be.
This combines present perfect with a definite past time and does not give the requested progressive.
pick.y: Be plus -ing gives the stated action in progress.

e: Use the participle written after has.
A singular third-person subject takes has.
The finite auxiliary is missing.
pick.y: Use has + past participle with this subject.

pick.q: Which word is an adjective in a careful learner?
e: Learner is the noun being described.
A is a determiner.
Carefully is not the adjective used in this phrase.
The simple-present form does not fit this completed-event model.
A finite verb is missing.
Use the past wrote here, not has plus wrote.
pick.y: The definite completed past context uses the simple past.
